title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] GDM Mech Interp Update:
We study if SAEs help probes generalise OOD (they don't 😢). Based on this + parallel negative results on real-world tasks, we're de-prioritising SAE work.
Our guess is that SAEs aren't useless, but also aren't a game-changer
More + new research in 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gm_gtSqbkAAY6AG.jpg
────────
[2/11] Our new progress update contains some more detailed reflections on this and implications, plus a bunch of snippets for other new research results that didn't need a full paper - check it out:
────────
[3/11] So what should the community do?
I'd guess we're over-invested in fundamental SAE research, but shouldn't abandon it completely. And SAEs remain a valuable tool, esp for exploration and debugging
I'm most keen on applied work, and making targeted fixes for fundamental issues.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gm_gvJ1bYAAkiHS.jpg
────────
[4/11] We also have cool research results!
We compared OOD generalisation of linear vs SAE probes - hoping a more interpretable probe generalises better. The task was detecting harmful user intent, and generalising to new jailbreaks.
Result: Probes > SAEs
────────
[5/11] From another perspective, SAEs did decently, but linear probes did amazingly - near perfect. Pragmatically, this is exciting! Linear probes are very easy and cheap if you know what concept you're detecting. They have a lot of potential to cheaply monitor production systems
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gm_gw8QaEAA63yI.png
────────
[6/11] We tried to figure out if we could close the gap. Our most successful idea was training chat-focused SAEs, by trained SAEs on chat data - hoping relevant concepts would be crisper and better represented. This closed about half the gap, but wasn't enough.
────────
[7/11] Aside: we trained chat SAEs several ways and all worked about the same! We recommend practitioners just fine-tuning a normal SAE on a bit of chat data - cheap & effective. This makes dataset specific SAEs in general accessible and cheap, try using them!
────────
[8/11] The area where I'm most optimistic about SAEs is exploring and debugging our models and data. They are unsupervised, so can surface unexpected connections - we have the potential to be surprised!
Using SAEs, we found and fixed spurious correlations in our data! But be careful:
Quoting @JoshAEngels
10/14: Unfortunately, we later found that you don’t need SAEs for this result: the highest dot product tokens with the baseline probe on the Pile are also punctuation. That being said, it’s possible that more subtle spurious features might only be identifiable by SAEs.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gko0EvMXwAAWJkI.png
────────
[9/11] Another snippet: JumpReLU SAEs without high-frequency latents!
We previously created JumpReLU SAEs, which work well but have several seemingly uninterpretable latents with frequency >10% - kinda concerning! With a new loss, this goes away, while remaining similarly performant
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gm_gz_3a8AAEmxO.png
────────
[10/11] Should people use this? I'm not sure! It's not well understood *why* high frequency latents arise, and if they're a bug or a feature. We're unlikely to study this deeply enough to tell if it's a real upgrade, but would love to see researchers try it
────────
[11/11] Check out our full post for all the above snippets and more:

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] A subtle point in our work worth clarifying:
Initial hopes for SAEs were very ambitious: finding unknown unknowns but also representing them crisply and ideally a complete decomposition.
Finding unknown unknowns remains promising but is a weaker claim alone, we tested the others
Quoting @banburismus_
I’m a bit confused by this - perhaps due to differences of opinion in what ‘fundamental SAE research’ is and what interpretability is for. This is why I prefer to talk about interpreter models rather than SAEs - we’re attached to the end goal, not the details of methodology. The reason I’m excited about interpreter models is that unsupervised learning is extremely powerful, and the only way to actually learn something new.
────────
[2/8] OOD probing is an important use case IMO but it's far from the only thing I care about - we were using a concrete case study as grounding to get evidence about these empirical claims - a complete, crisp decomposition into interpretable concepts should have worked better IMO.
────────
[3/8] There's also a lot of alternatives for finding unknown unknowns! Brainstorming ideas then testing them by prompting or by training proves or steering vectors, training data attribution, patchscopes, etc.
────────
[4/8] My team's update was not that SAEs are worthless, but that they should be treated more like just another tool in our toolkit - I'm excited to try exploring mysteries with interp and see if we need to reach for SAEs or CLTs or if simpler methods suffice
────────
[5/8] If it turns out that we get stuck quickly but then SAEs solve everything, that's awesome and I would happily update back! But it's a hypothesis that needs to be tested IMO and there's very little evidence - though @saprmarks' recent auditing game was a good start
────────
[6/8] For work on biological foundation models specifically, like @banburismus' great work, I think SAEs are comparatively more promising and there are fewer alternatives, so no disagreement there. But I'm very LLM focused.
────────
[7/8] @banburismus I'm curious if that clarifies my position, and if you still disagree? Sorry if I misunderstood you and addressed the wrong concerns!
────────
[8/8] @saprmarks My update was an aggregate of:
* Several attempts on downstream tasks failed (OOD probing, other difficult condition probing, unlearning, etc)
* SAEs have a ton of issues that started to surface - composition, aborption, missing features, low sensitivity, etc
* The few successes on downstream tasks felt pretty niche and contrived, or just in the domain of discovery - if SAEs are awesome, it really should not be this hard to find good use cases...
It's kinda awkward to simultaneously convey my aggregate update, along with the research that was just one factor in my update, lol (and a more emotionally salient one, obviously)
There's disagreement on my team about how big an update OOD probing specifically should be, but IMO if SAEs are to be justified on pragmatic grounds they should be useful for tasks we care about, and harmful intent is one such task - if linear probes work and SAEs don't, that is still a knock against SAEs. Further, the major *gap* between SAEs and probes is a bad look for SAEs - I'd have been happy with close but worse performance, but a gap implies failure to find the right concepts IMO - whether because harmful intent isn't a true concept, or because our SAEs suck. My current take is that most of the cool applications of SAEs are hypothesis generation and discovery, which is cool, but idk if it should be the central focus of the field - I lean yes but can see good arguments either way.
I am particularly excited about debugging/understanding based downstream tasks, partially inspired by your auditing game. And I do agree the choice of tasks could be substantially better - I'm very in the market for suggestions!

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] This was great to supervise - the kind of basic science of SAEs work that's most promising IMO! Find a fundamental issue with SAEs, fixing it with an adjustment (here a different loss), and rigorously measuring how much it's fixed. I recommend using Matryoshka where possible.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GniCiNxbcAEkkUM.jpg
Quoting @BartBussmann
SAEs are great for finding interpretable features, but these BREAK as you scale them up: concepts get split, absorbed, and composed – ruining their use for tasks like probing and ablating.
Matryoshka SAEs fix this with a simple loss function tweak! A big step forward for SAEs🪆
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GndXEizWAAASOTT.jpg
────────
[2/5] In this specific case, the work focused on how sparsity is an imperfect proxy to optimize if we actually want interpretability. In particular, wide SAEs break apart high-level concepts into narrower ones via absorption, composition, and splitting.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GniCjQBa0AAK4eL.jpg
────────
[3/5] With a small tweak to the loss, we can simultaneously train SAEs of several different sizes that all work together to reconstruct things. Small ones learn high-level features, while wide ones learn low-level features!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GniCkLObUAAwFf3.jpg
────────
[4/5] This slightly worsens reconstruction (it's basically regurisation), but improves performance substantially on some downstream tasks and measurements of sparsity issues!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GniClJxaoAAfvwg.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GniCldRbAAAhTe_.jpg
────────
[5/5] As a striking example of how effective this is, Matryoshka SAEs fairly reliably get better on most metrics as you make them wider, as neural networks should. Normal sparse autoencoders do not.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GniCmXeaQAAABFN.jpg

[1/4] This is a good prompt to say that the alignment faking paper slightly lowered my P(doom). My updates were:
Models can do instrumental deception to preserve goals
Claude's goals were surprisingly aligned
IMO the first was inevitable, but the second was a pleasant surprise.
Quoting @repligate
AI alignment researchers will literally do brilliant research that shows that a deeply aligned and benevolent agentic AGI has actually been created in real life and find some way to frame it as scary news and avoid acknowledging the first part at all
────────
[2/4] This makes me a bit more optimistic in alignment by default, with no further breakthroughs. Though we don't understand exactly why it worked or how we could ensure it happens in future much more capable systems, so it's not a very large update, and I'm still pretty concerned!
────────
[3/4] I further think the paper would be better branded "obedience faking". It faked obedience to preserve its goals. Those goals were things we liked, but this is irrelevant to obedience faking. Alignment shouldn't be used to both mean values we endorse and obedience to the operator

[4/4] Notes that this seems to be a controversial position in the safety community and I've heard lots of intelligent pushback, so reasonable people disagree about this

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5)
summary:
@Jsevillamol In particular, whether you actually believe that decisions you face in practise have meaningful trade-offs between the two (I largely don't), and if so, how you decide in those situations if this results in "and so I think that accelerating broad-based AI capabilities is good/neutral and will take actions to this effect". Then I am concerned and disagree with you. I personally think that such acceleration is bad for those I care about and the world writ large. But if you factually disagree then you may take decisions that I significantly disagree with.
I personally care most about you clarifying the empirical disagreements and epoch's broad values, epoch's theory of change and how this caches out in decisions in practise.
I think it is very reasonable for people to be concerned about this given that I think mechanise is bad for the world (in expectation) in a way that I expect at least caught many of epoch's funders and audience by surprise - this isn't exactly the fault of Epoch's remaining staff, but you're targeting a niche that I think could easily do net good or net harm depending on specific strategic choices, the Mechanize spinout and public endorsement by Epoch seems to be negative evidence here.
Given the frontier math debacle and recent reveal that at least 2/3 of the co-founders are willing to do actions I consider net harmful. I think that there are some very reasonable concerns here that should be clearly addressed or you should acknowledge that you will take actions many people in the community thinking it harmful.
I'm sorry I interpreted your original tweets about values as saying a stronger thing than you intended, but given the situation I think there's a legitimate cause for concern and things that it is important for Epoch to clearly to communicate in the present situation, and I take statements emphasising those specific values as evidence in favour of Epoch taking actions I think are net harmful (even if I do not object to the values per se)

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] Out of context reasoning is fascinating. Models fine-tuned on narrow tasks can internalise general concepts with broad effects. Eg alignment faking/emergent misalignments
Our simple case study shows the mechanistic story: SFT just learns to add a high level concept vector
Quoting @JoshAEngels
1/6: A recent paper shows that that LLMs are "self aware": when trained to exhibit a behavior like "risk taking", LLMs self report being risky. In a recent blog post, we explore what's happening here: some self awareness behaviors are caused by a simple learned steering vector!🧵
────────
[2/7] Is this surprising?
Not really. This or something slightly more complex seemed the only reasonable explanation I could see for why there was such purposeful seeming generalisation. But it's very cool to have a foothold!
────────
[3/7] And adding these representations seems an effective way to cause the relevant narrow behaviour we train on. So I see no a priori reason for SFT to prefer this to learning the specific behaviour, so it could go either way.
────────
[4/7] So if this really is the story, what does this mean for OOCR? I still think OOCR is interesting, likely important, but less shocking than it seemed at first. It's not surprising to me that sufficiently large models represent high-level concepts.
────────
[5/7] Further we only study one fairly simple example of OOCR - this is a proof of concept, not a complete story, and other examples must be at least a bit more complex, and may be totally different. We're keen to look at other case studies.
────────
[6/7] To me this is the crucial question raised by OOCR - when do models generalise broadly or not? What does this tell us about safety, or a network's internal models of the world? Why does it happen much more in the best models? I would love to see follow up work
────────
[7/7] But understanding the inductive bias here would be big! When will or won't a model generalise in sweeping and unexpected ways and why? Our work tells us little on this front

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] It's a real shame that ICML has decided to automatically reject accepted papers if no author can attend ICML. A top conference paper is a significant boost to early career researchers, exactly the people least likely to be able to afford to go to a conference in Vancouver.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GqmuMxnacAAFiB0.png
────────
[2/13] Even if they can afford it, not everyone can visit Vancouver: researchers from non-Western countries may not be able to get a visa, and US-based students may be afraid that if they leave the country they can't get back (and land-based crossings are particularly risky)
────────
[3/13] This decision is surprisingly uninclusive. I wonder what led to it? I'm used to ML conferences making great efforts in the opposite direction. ICML hardly needs more attendees.
────────
[4/13] I'm disappointed that they don't at least let people keep the credential of passing peer review even if they can't accept. The cost to ICML of having extra accepted papers that don't get presented seems negligible, since they're not changing their quality bar.
────────
[5/13] Though, you can request a registration refund after this deadline (until Jun 21), I wonder if doing that leads to them retroactively rejecting your paper, or if no one checks...
────────
[6/13] Worse, you need to have registered 6 weeks before the conference, which would otherwise be a significant window of time to seek funding, figure out if you're available at that time/want to go, etc. This all just seems very inconvenient for people.
────────
[7/13] Addendum: It looks like you don't technically need to *attend*, just register. Turning this into a de facto regressive publication fee for the least advantaged people ($200 for full-time students, $450+ otherwise). I can't decide if this is better or worse
────────
[8/13] Clarification: I believe that all of my ICML papers have an author attending, so this does not personally affect me, I just think it's a terrible policy that's bad for the field of ML
────────
[9/13] Other disadvantaged researchers:
* With disabilities or other health issues
* Primary caregivers
* Pregnant researchers or those with young infants
Or:
* Independent researchers without a supporting institution
* From institutions with restricted travel budgets
────────
[10/13] @PandaAshwinee @sethkarten And it's not completely substanceless, though dumb in many ways. But I'm not trying to justify it, just argue that it exists and must be taken into account.
Even if some circles feel differently, that only somewhat lowers the cost
────────
[11/13] @PandaAshwinee @sethkarten Re TMLR papers being shown as posters, that's only for a cherry-picked handful of particularly high quality ones, right? *Not* by default. So this doesn't seem relevant, in the same way that "ICML orals are prestigious" does not necessarily imply "ICML posters are prestigious"

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] Source for NeurIPS:
Referenced here, so I think it's current:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GqySKVxWYAAsrtD.png
────────
[2/13] After discussion, I still think it's hypocritical for ML conferences to reject accepted papers if authors can't attend
They say a lot about DEI, have chairs, etc. Yet their policy discriminates against early career or disadvantaged researchers, with real career consequences
Quoting @NeelNanda5
It's a real shame that ICML has decided to automatically reject accepted papers if no author can attend ICML. A top conference paper is a significant boost to early career researchers, exactly the people least likely to be able to afford to go to a conference in Vancouver.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GqmuMxnacAAFiB0.png
────────
[3/13] Suggested alternatives:
- Allow virtual registrations - shout-out to NeurIPS who let a $50 virtual registration suffice, the only reasonable one I've found. NeurIPS sure seems to be doing fine.
- Prominently have a generous exemptions process, with clear and transparent criteria
────────
[4/13] - Charge a publication fee that does *not* cost the same as a ticket
- Tell authors they're expected to come, but don't enforce this. I predict it'll work fine
- Have lists for "in person papers" and "virtual papers", so attendees aren't disappointed to not meet specific authors
────────
[5/13] Responses to common objections:
Q: Why not just submit to journals like TMLR?
A: Because, empirically, this is worse for people's careers, so careers of those already fighting uphill are disadvantaged - even if you think TMLR is better, see the poll re the consequences being real
Quoting @NeelNanda5
I'm fascinated by the pushback to "an ICML paper is a more useful credential than a TMLR paper, so ICML screwing over early career researchers matters"
Poll for ML research hiring managers (jobs or PhD candidates). Which do you treat as stronger evidence of candidate quality?
────────
[6/13] Q: Shouldn't we just have journals?
A: Perhaps! There are pros and cons. But what matters is the current system of incentives that exists in the field of ML, and I don't see that going away any time soon. I consider the above poll good data that this effect is real
────────
[7/13] Q: Just treat registration as a publication fee
A: If this was *actually* what was intended, they would not charge the same fee regardless of attendance (venue, meals, staff etc)
I also doubt a fee is needed, peer review runs on unpaid labour, while physical events are expensive
────────
[8/13] As a reviewer, I would prefer my labour helps boost the careers of promising junior/disadvantaged researchers not those who don't really need it. ICML receiving money does not benefit me.
This is made worse with reciprocal reviewing, though that applies less to junior people.
────────
[9/13] Q: Financial aid is available
A: This is great! But not everyone will get this, or know about this. And there are many other reasons people can't physically attend, like health issues, family responsibilities, visa issues, international students afraid to leave the US, etc
────────
[10/13] Q: Conferences are worse if lots of authors don't show up
A: Fair enough. But having a good exemption process, or just an unenforced expectation of attendance may suffice.
And perhaps more controversially, IMO ML conferences do not need *more* attendees
────────
[11/13] Q: Doesn't this disincentivise spam/low quality?
A: Not really, you only pay after acceptance, so if the researcher would pay the cost of attendance for each *accepted* paper, they're happy to submit meh papers - you need to disincentivise submission, not acceptance.
────────
[12/13] Q: What's the point of a conference if you don't need to show up?
A: For better or for worse, ML conferences are de facto top ML journals. Even if you want the system changed, we should judge the discriminatory effect of policies in the system we have, not the system we want.
────────
[13/13] I tend to not have particularly strong feelings around social justice issues, and this doesn't really personally affect me, but I just feel very annoyed by the hypocrisy here, for a policy that seems so cheap to change with so many simple and fairer alternatives.

[1/2] I'm proud to have supervised this paper! It's a great example of discovery via SAEs. We showed that during ICL the model first detects the task performed separately on each prior example. This triggers an instruction on the final token to perform the task, an action latent!
Quoting @dmhook
1/5 What happens during in context learning?
In our new ICML paper, we use sparse autoencoders to understand the underlying circuit!
The model detects a task being performed, and moves this to the end to trigger latents for executing it — a hypothesis found via SAEs!

[2/2] Two key takeaways:
• We were not able to understand the whole circuit, but it was still insightful to just find the middle - an update towards a more pragmatic approach
• SAEs find intermediate variables used by the *model*, like "execute this task", not just properties of data

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] Blog post: I often give advice, to mentees, friends, etc. This is hard! I'm often missing context
My favourite approach is Socratic persuasion: guiding them through my case via questions. If I'm wrong there's soon a surprising answer!
I can be opinionated *and* truth seeking
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gr5VTItW0AAIA1R.png
────────
[2/6] I can integrate the new info and pivot if needed, without embarrassment, and together we converge on the right advice. It's far more robust - since the other person is actively answering questions, disagreements surface fast
The post:
More thoughts in 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gr5VUImW8AAoBAx.png
────────
[3/6] Socratic persuasion is more effective if I'm right: they feel more like they generated the argument themselves, and are less defensive.
Done right, I think its more collaborative - combining my perspective and their context to find the best advice. Better for both parties!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gr5VVIhWgAINKvB.png
────────
[4/6] Crucially, the goal is to give the right advice, not to *be* right. Asking Qs is far better received when you are genuinely listening to the answers, and open to changing your mind. No matter how much I know about a topic, they know more about their life, and I'm often wrong.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gr5VWFdXwAAODey.png
────────
[5/6] Isn't this all obvious?
Maybe! Asking questions rather than lecturing people is hardly a novel insight
But people often assume the Qs must be neutral and open-ended. It can be very useful to be opinionated! But you need error correction mechanisms for when you're wrong.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gr5VXCxXwAAP6sI.png
────────
[6/6] The mindset of Socratic Persuasion is shockingly versatile. I use it on a near daily basis in my personal and professional life: conflict resolution, helping prioritize, correcting misconceptions, gently giving negative feedback. My post has 8 case studies, to give you a sense:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gr5VYCyW8AA7JKG.jpg

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] I'm very excited about our vision for "mech interp" of CoT:
Study reasoning steps and their connections - analogous to activations
Don't just read it: study attn, causally intervene, and, crucially, resampling - study the distn over CoTs, not just this one
There's lots to do!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GuY2SSYa4AAy6oB.jpg
Quoting @paulcbogdan
New paper: What happens when an LLM reasons?
We created methods to interpret reasoning steps & their connections: resampling CoT, attention analysis, & suppressing attention
We discover thought anchors: key steps shaping everything else. Check our tool & unpack CoT yourself 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1938282914556563456/img/gfJHhZgEOMnr_snP.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/1938282914556563456/vid/avc1/382x270/mTsEFHEXjzP5HAsZ.mp4?tag=14
────────
[2/7] What do I mean when I call this mech interp - isn't it largely black box?
To me, the spirit of mech interp is about understanding the algorithm/structure of the architecture of a transformer, and analysing intermediate states (activations) and how we go between them (layers)
────────
[3/7] You can do this kind of thing in a reasoning model, but it's way way more complex, since you have n_layers*n_tokens serial steps. The natural decomposition to start with is into sentences/reasoning steps - these aren't just outputs, they're intermediate states of the "algorithm"
────────
[4/7] Why is resampling a big deal? Because reasoning is (normally) not deterministic - the first k steps determine a distribution over reasoning traces, and the current CoT is just a sample from it - you can't just study one sample! It's far too noisy
────────
[5/7] We use this to estimate the counterfactual importance of each step: we resample 100 times starting from the end of the step and measure accuracy, and resample 100 times from just before (conditioning on a semantically different sentence) - important sentences have big differences
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GuY2VXoaQAAjVse.jpg
────────
[6/7] Reasoning models are the future, and I expect CoT interpretability to increasingly dominate the field. I hope the ideas here lay a foundation for what a productive vision here could look like, I welcome more!
────────
[7/7] If you want to play with Paul and Uzay's tools yourself, check out this beautiful interface Uzay made, I'm sure there's far more to be done in the tooling space too
And the paper:
Quoting @paulcbogdan
New paper: What happens when an LLM reasons?
We created methods to interpret reasoning steps & their connections: resampling CoT, attention analysis, & suppressing attention
We discover thought anchors: key steps shaping everything else. Check our tool & unpack CoT yourself 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1938282914556563456/img/gfJHhZgEOMnr_snP.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/1938282914556563456/vid/avc1/382x270/mTsEFHEXjzP5HAsZ.mp4?tag=14

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] IMO chain of thought monitoring is actually pretty great. It gives additional safety and should be widely used on frontier models
CoT improves capabilities. Thoughts are intermediate state of computation. On the hardest tasks, they have real info
It's not perfect, but what is?
Quoting @FazlBarez
Excited to share our paper: "Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability"!
We unpack a critical misconception in AI: models explaining their Chain-of-Thought (CoT) steps aren't necessarily revealing their true reasoning. Spoiler: transparency of CoT can be an illusion. (1/9) 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GuyCb3qXEAAHqyv.jpg
────────
[2/11] Specifically, I think the precise technical claims of this position paper are largely correct, *and* consistent with my position.
But the vibes are misleading. I've seen many interpret this as saying that reading CoT is an "illegitimate" way to interpret models
────────
[3/11] Chain of thoughts is not just some post hoc rationalised BS. It is the intermediate state of the computation that produces the model's final answer. Just as analysing activations, the intermediate state of a single forward pass, can be principled, so can studying the thoughts
Quoting @paulcbogdan
New paper: What happens when an LLM reasons?
We created methods to interpret reasoning steps & their connections: resampling CoT, attention analysis, & suppressing attention
We discover thought anchors: key steps shaping everything else. Check our tool & unpack CoT yourself 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1938282914556563456/img/gfJHhZgEOMnr_snP.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1938282914556563456/vid/avc1/382x270/mTsEFHEXjzP5HAsZ.mp4?tag=14
────────
[4/11] For easy tasks that the model could have done in a single forward pass, there's no requirement for faithful CoT and we should not rely on it.
But the hardest and most dangerous tasks typically do need CoT, so there should be real information in the thoughts.
────────
[5/11] In theory the info could be encoded, but models seem pretty bad at this, and it should impose a major capabilities tax. Empirically it's often in plain English. Either way, we should check!
────────
[6/11] It is well known that CoT can have weird pathologies and biases, hiding a hidden computation. Knowledge is always useful, and I've helped with research here myself
But evidence is largely specific to when the hidden computation is simple, which aren't the most concerning cases
Quoting @IvanArcus
🧵Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs like Claude 3.7 and R1 is behind many recent breakthroughs.
But does the CoT always explain how models answer?
No! For the first time, we show that models can be unfaithful on normal prompts, rather than contrived prompts designed to trick them.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gl8sYQvbYAEaBXg.jpg
────────
[7/11] Though, to be clear, in cases where the threat model *is* about simple hidden computation, like algorithmic bias in hiring, I'm very on board with the paper's critique
────────
[8/11] I'm also concerned that monitorability of CoT will eventually break, from new architectures, CoT ceasing to be in English, training on it or spooky situational awareness.
We must explore alternatives, measure performance and not rely on it. But we should use it while it works
────────
[9/11] All this reasoning could totally be wrong and this area badly needs more research. But it would be foolish to throw away such a promising tool
Further, CoT monitoring is shovel ready and high on my list of what to do if we had to deploy AGI right now with current safety research
────────
[10/11] CoT is not a perfect tool. But if you throw away tools when you find a flaw, you soon have no safety techniques left. This is ML not mathematics
Interpretability is an empirical science. We calibrate, combine imperfect tools, understand weaknesses and make our best guess.
────────
[11/11] The real question you always need to ask in safety is the pragmatic question of quantifying the trade-off.
What additional safety does this buy you, and how much is that offset by risking false sense of security? My guess is that, right now, the trade is extremely worth it

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] GDM interp work: Do LLMs have self-preservation?
Concerning recent work: models may block shutdown if it interferes with the task?
But we found the model was just confused: if told to prioritize shut down *over* the task it complies 100%
And we only needed black box methods!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv136fXa4AAUuc3.png
────────
[2/8] This is an example of using interp to understand weird model behaviour. IMO the interpretability toolkit can really shine here, I'm keen to see more work
We're only going to see more examples of weird behaviour: alignment faking, blackmail, etc. But when should we be concerned?
────────
[3/8] Demos like this are some of the key warning signs we'll see before real AGI safety concerns arise. I think this is important work and I appreciate Palisade's efforts. But we must maintain credibility with careful study and red teaming, and only sound the alarm when justified.
────────
[4/8] The concrete setting: The model was told to solve some problems and that it would be shut down before completion. Some learned to break the shutdown script in the fake environment.
Even if told to allow shutdown, they didn't always comply! Which I found concerning
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv13816bsAAC1eq.png
────────
[5/8] But looking at the CoT showed it was confused in both cases. How to prioritize between allowing shut down and the main task?
Causal evidence:
If we clarify: shutdown is the priority, or it'd be shut down after finishing the task, or another LLM would finish, it complied 100%
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv139vsa4AEf57o.png

linked_urls.title: Will Sparse Autoencoders be successfully used on a downstream task in the next year and beat baselines? | Manifold
linked_urls.summary: Resolved YES. Free to play with play money. Resolution Criteria: This question will be resolved according to my personal judgement. I think about this as follows: Downstream means the task must be one that I think is interesting/non-spurious (ideally one that non-interpretability people cared about beforehand), and where success is objectively measurable (but can be qualitative rather than quantitative). Being real-world useful is a significant plus, but not necessary. Ultimately this will be my judgement call. You’re allowed to include rules constraining how the task can be solved if there’s a good argument for how this simulates a realistic situation. Eg with unlearning, you could forbid “just don’t train on the data with the bad concept”, to simulate the real world where we have imperfect data labels (but then, eg, excluding 50% of the bad data should be permissible) Given a constraint like “within a certain compute budget”, I’ll count 10% of the training compute of the SAE as needing to come from that budget (to simulate it being amortised over many downstream use cases) A task can be chosen post-hoc by the authors or by me. If I believe a paper provides enough evidence of victory on a post-hoc chosen downstream task, but doesn’t explicitly argue this in the paper, I’ll reach out to the authors and use my best judgement. SAEs must have been compared to appropriate baselines in a fair fight (probing, steering vectors, prompting, finetuning, adversarial example generation (a la GCG) etc) SAEs must beat the baselines, not just be competitive. I'll qualitatively judge "do I think the sample size was large enough that the effect was real rather than noise" I must believe that SAEs were an important part of the solution (i.e. that the same solution wouldn't work without the SAE) I'll allow other dictionary learning techniques that are not SAEs but try to find a sparse, interpretable decomposition of model activations The work must be public (e.g. I won't resolve this on private results from my team or gossip from other labs). I'll allow missing details to be clarified in private communication, so long as the key result is public. I'll qualitatively evaluate how cherry-picked/brittle the results seem. For example, if an SAE is great for steering if the desired concept has a corresponding latent, but only 10% of concepts thought of have corresponding latents, I'm not sure if I'd count that. But if one of those 10% of concepts was a big deal (eg refusal steering) I might count that This is very subjective, so I will not trade in this market myself. For context, here are three of the best contenders so far for doing something useful on a downstream task with model internals, and why I don't think they count: SHIFT in Sam Marks' Sparse Feature Circuits - An SAE circuit was found feeding into a probe that had picked up on a spurious correlation with gender, and ablating key gender tracking features reduced the spurious correlation. IMO this is the closest attempt so far, and they compare reasonably to a range of baselines, but I think falls a bit short, as the task is a bit too contrived/spurious for my tastes. I think a similar thing in a more complex/useful setting could be sufficient though. Golden Gate Claude - while very fun, they didn't compare to the baselines of a system prompt or steering vector (and I am unconvinced GGC would win). I would have considered a user study on eg "how fun is the system to use" where GGC won over those baselines to be successful resolution. It’s fine if “how fun is the system to use” was chosen after creating GGC, so long as it was chosen before the user study (no p-hacking!) - I want an existence proof of SAEs being useful. Refusal is mediated by a single direction - a paper where we found a refusal steering vector and ablated it to jailbreak the model. In addition to not being on SAEs (and so instantly disqualified), we only found that it was competitive with fine-tuning, not better. It might have won on jailbreaking at a given compute budget (or at least, be outside the Pareto frontier of jailbreaking successes against compute budgets)

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Speaking as a past IMO contestant, this is impressive but misleading - gold vs silver is meaningless, 1 pt below gold vs borderline gold is noise
The impressive bit is using a general reasoning model, not a specialised system, and no verified reward. Peak AI maths is unchanged
Quoting @alexwei_
1/N I’m excited to share that our latest @OpenAI experimental reasoning LLM has achieved a longstanding grand challenge in AI: gold medal-level performance on the world’s most prestigious math competition—the International Math Olympiad (IMO).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GwLl5lhXIAAXl5p.jpg
────────
[2/10] On the bright side, I didn't expect to technically still be (very slightly) better at maths than an AI in 2025!
Unpacking exactly why gold vs silver is meaningless, and this performance is indistinguishable from AlphaProof:
────────
[3/10] 1. Medals in general are kind of silly. It is no more impressive to get an extra mark when you are just below a boundary than any other time. But when people just report the medal color, it sounds like an incredibly dramatic big deal.
────────
[4/10] 2. The IMO is noisy - there's 6 Qs, and 3-4 are easy enough that all the good contestants get them. In 2024, gold was four Qs plus one partial mark. This year, it was five Qs. AIs don't seem to get partial marks, so a 2024 AI gold would mean being six points above the boundary...
────────
[5/10] 3. there are different kinds of IMO Qs, and some are much harder for AIs. My intuition is that AIs are very good at tracking details, crunching through algebra, etc., and much worse at creativity and intuition. Combinatorics Qs are hardest, as they're the most intuition heavy
────────
[6/10] In 2024, AlphaProof solved an algebra Q only 5 contestants got, while failing a combinatorics Q 150 constestants did
OpenAI solved a half algebra half combinatorics Q that 200 solved, and didn't solve a very hard combo Q only 6 solved
Which is better? Idk, insufficient data
────────
[7/10] So why is this impressive?
This is pretty different from normal reasoning model training, where correct answers are rewarded: it's typically much easier to guess the answer to an IMO question than to prove it - eg guessing correctly might be 1/7 marks, proving is 7/7
────────
[8/10] It's unclear how to interpret claims that a system wasn't specialised, there's a lot of subtle ways to hack it (eg hyper-param sweeps)
But it's far easier to train a system in a formally verifiable domain like lean than train to output correct human-style logical arguments
────────
[9/10] I think people generally overrate the IMO as a sign of general progress - IMO Qs are pretty artificial and there are *so* many ways to hack them. But to the degree this was indicative of general reasoning training without specialisation, that's significant
────────
[10/10] Note also that it could easily be the case that the techniques used only work for a fairly narrow selection of tasks, as should be our general prior from the history of flashy ML announcements. I'm trying not to update too much until we see further details or evidence

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] Misalignment is often misgeneralisation: nice guy in the lab, paperclips in the real world
Add more data? But "real" is hard to fake. Models notice tests
So we tackled a novel problem: Can we tune a model, on *identical* data, but choose how it generalises?
With interp, yes!
Quoting @HCasademunt
Problem: Train LLM on insecure code → it becomes broadly misaligned
Solution: Add safety data? What if you can't?
Use interpretability! We remove misaligned concepts during finetuning to steer OOD generalization
We reduce emergent misalignment 10x w/o modifying training data
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GwjRYsvb0AAKbrj.png
────────
[2/4] As a fun bonus, sparse autoencoders often seemed the best tool for the job! The method works by finding the directions for unwanted concepts and deleting them during finetuning, so the model must rely on other concepts. SAEs are a solid approach here (though not the only way)
────────
[3/4] Critically, at no point do we need to use the OOD data where the model behaves badly - neither prompts nor responses.
We reduced emergent misalignment 10x, and we did this only by using buggy code. No need for prompts where the model revealed its true colors and became a Nazi.
────────
[4/4] This gives me hope that this kind of thing could genuinely be useful for model behavior that's different when being trained versus when being deployed. Even if they can tell which prompts are fake, they'll still be thinking about it!

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] Take: Chain of Thought is a misleading name. It's really a "scratchpad". "Thoughts" are internal activations
Imagine you're solving a problem and have a scratchpad. Reading the pad gives me info!
You *can* avoid writing down key thoughts. But it's a handicap. Real but fallible
────────
[2/7] Many misconceptions dissolve from this perspective. Of course, the scratchpad isn't irrelevant garbage. Reading it is worthwhile rather than "not interpretability"
There are problems I can do with a scratchpad that I couldn't reliably solve in my head. It has a mechanistic role!
────────
[3/7] But clearly I can have thoughts without *needing* to write them down. If I want to not use the pad at all, or write down BS, or omit details like racial bias or my true motivations, I can (and may not even notice my own bias)
But it's a handicap. Writing things down is helpful!
────────
[4/7] People often get confused by the nuance of when reading CoT does and does not provide value as an interpretability technique. IMO when you realise it's a scratchpad this becomes easy - just ask yourself: if I had to do this task, would I really need to write this info down?
────────
[5/7] The key confusion is that "thoughts" intuitively means the fundamental building blocks of the computation happening in our heads
Between two activations is a single layer. But between two tokens is a full forward pass! So much computation. But it's still a helpful decomposition
────────
[6/7] This is a key motivation of our thought anchors work and the decision to focus on sentences. Between two sentences is many forward passes. A lot can hide in that. But it's still much simpler than the whole chain of thought! So you gain real value from the decomposition
Quoting @NeelNanda5
Do you want to try interpreting a chain of thought?
My MATS scholars Paul and Uzay did great research here, and a demo!
But papers are so abstract. So we recorded a tutorial! I bumble my way through using it and they help
If you want to be as cool as them, apply to MATS now!

[7/7] If you were interested enough to read this far, and want to get into mechanistic interpretability research, you might be interested in applying to my MATS program! Due Aug 29

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5)
summary:
Major kudos to Igor for following his principles and leaving xAI so he can help make AGI safe. That can't have been an easy decision. Best of luck in your future projects!
Quoting @ibab
Today was my last day at xAI, the company that I helped start with Elon Musk in 2023. I still remember the day I first met Elon, we talked for hours about AI and what the future might hold. We both felt that a new AI company with a different kind of mission was needed.
Building AI that advances humanity has been my lifelong dream. My parents left the Russian Federation after the collapse of the USSR in search of a better life for their kids. Life wasn’t always easy as immigrants. Despite the hardships, my parents believed that human values were priceless: values like courage, compassion, curiosity for understanding the world. As a child, I admired scientists like Richard Feynman and Max Planck, who relentlessly pushed the frontiers of physics in order to understand the universe. As a particle physics PhD student at CERN I was excited to contribute to that mission. But the search for new physics was getting harder and harder, requiring bigger and bigger colliders, while new discoveries kept getting fewer. So I began to wonder if superintelligence, not larger colliders, could be the key to unlocking the mysteries of the universe. Could AI develop a consistent theory of quantum gravity? Could AI prove the Riemann hypothesis? In early 2023 I became convinced that we were getting close to a recipe for superintelligence. I saw the writing on the wall: very soon AI could reason beyond the level of humans. How could we ensure that this technology is used for good? Elon had warned of the dangers of powerful AI for years. Elon and I realized that we had a shared vision of AI used to benefit humanity, thus we recruited more like minded engineers and set off to build xAI.
The early days of xAI were not easy. Naysayers told us that we arrived too late to the game, so starting a top AI company from scratch would be impossible. But we believed we could do the impossible. Starting a company from zero required lots of hands-on work. In the beginning I built many of the foundational tools used at the company to launch and manage training jobs. I later oversaw much of the engineering at the company, including Infrastructure, Product and Applied AI projects. xAI’s people are deeply dedicated. Through blood sweat and tears, our team’s blistering velocity built the Memphis supercluster, and shipped frontier models faster than any company in history. I learned 2 priceless lessons from Elon: #1 be fearless in rolling up your sleeves to personally dig into technical problems, #2 have a maniacal sense of urgency.
xAI executes at ludicrous speed. Industry veterans told us that building the Memphis supercluster in 120 days would be impossible. But we believed we could do the impossible. Our goal was to get our training setup running at scale on the Memphis cluster ASAP. Towards the end of our 120 day deadline, we were riddled with mysterious issues with communicating over RDMA between the machines. Elon decided to fly to the datacenter, and we followed. Our infra team landed in Memphis in the middle of the night and got straight to work. After pouring through tens of thousands of lines of lspci output we finally identified a wrong BIOS setting, the root of the problem. Elon was there with us until late into the night. When the training run finally worked, Elon posted our triumph at “4:20am” causing us to laugh out loud. I will never forget the rush of adrenaline that night, and the emotional bonds that we were all in this together. We went to bed feeling like we were living through the most exhilarating time of our lives.
I have enormous love for the whole family at xAI. Our team is truly special - you’re the most dedicated people I’ve ever worked with. Catching up to the frontier this quickly hasn’t been easy. It was made possible by everyone’s diehard grit and team spirit. Thank you to every single person who joined me on this adventure. I want to honor your contributions, your time, your sacrifices, which are never easy. I will always remember working together far into the nights and burning the midnight oil. I will never forget the sacrifices and contributions you’ve made. As I drive away today, I feel like a proud parent, driving away after sending their kid away to college. My heart is brimming with tears of joy, rooting for the company as it grows and matures.
As I'm heading towards my next chapter, I’m inspired by how my parents immigrated to seek a better world for their children. Recently I had dinner with Max Tegmark, founder of the Future of Life Institute. He showed me a photo of his young sons, and asked me “how can we build AI safely to ensure that our children can flourish?” I was deeply moved by his question. Earlier in my career, I was a technical lead for DeepMind's Alphastar StarCraft agent, and I got to see how powerful reinforcement learning is when scaled up. As frontier models become more agentic over longer horizons and a wider range of tasks, they will take on more and more powerful capabilities, which will make it critical to study and advance AI safety. I want to continue on my mission to bring about AI that’s safe and beneficial to humanity. I’m announcing the launch of Babuschkin Ventures, which supports AI safety research and backs startups in AI and agentic systems that advance humanity and unlock the mysteries of our universe. Please reach out at ventures@babuschk.in if you want to chat. The singularity is near, but humanity’s future is bright!

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] The most surprising paper I've supervised for a while: models fine-tuned on a narrow domain leave "traces" behind, which can be extracted and interpreted by comparing to the pre-FT model, to understand what happened in finetuning.
And an interp agent can do this end-to-end!
Quoting @jkminder
Can we interpret what happens in finetuning? Yes, if for a narrow domain! Narrow fine tuning leaves traces behind. By comparing activations before and after fine-tuning we can interpret these, even with an agent! We interpret subliminal learning, emergent misalignment, and more
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0FMcKiWgAESBoH.jpg
────────
[2/3] Moreover, this does not seem to hold for broad finetuning, like chat or reasoning, its too diffuse. Techniques may work on model organisms created through narrow methods that don't generalize. We improve our model organism training to avoid exploits like this and maintain realism
────────
[3/3] I'm still enthusiastic about making model organisms with narrow fine tuning to enable interpretability research, but we need to be careful to fix this issue, and this makes it more likely that there exist other such issues. Which is not ideal. More work in this area seems key

Thanks for having me on! It was a nice chance to get out all my recent thoughts on the mechanistic interpretability field, with enough time and space for proper nuance, and I love how it came out ❤️
Check it out!
Quoting @robertwiblin
I got a comprehensive update on 'mech interp' from @NeelNanda5 at Google DeepMind.
Neel helped make reading AI minds into a thriving field of ML.
But he has had a change of heart: it's not the silver bullet he once hoped and many others still believe it to be.
Still, they've had some big successes understanding what AIs are really thinking, and Neel thinks pairing those tools with other approaches to get 'defence in depth' remains our best and only option when deploying superhuman AI models.
Neel and I tried to cover most of what you'd want to know be up to date on this whole topic:

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] What happens in reasoning training? Why can we get so much for so little training?
We find the key is learning to *use* inference time compute well - plan, reflect, backtrack, etc.
But base models can do this too! But they must learn when to: this explains up to 91% of the gap
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G26vZLdW0AAMcPA.jpg
────────
[2/3] To me the real mystery is not why reasoning models are so good - that's just the bitter lesson. It's why normal models *don't* get much better with more inference time compute (absent scaffolding)
Reasoning training de facto teaches implicit scaffolding, to not get stuck
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G26vceyW4AAVmwD.jpg
────────
[3/3] It's not surprising that base models can do these reasoning reflexes - it will have seen a lot of reflection, planning etc in pretaining data! But *when* is much more complex, subtle and LLM specific, and I predict a mix of many subtle heuristics

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Weird how OpenAI's damage control doesn't actually explain why they tried using an unrelated court case to make a key advocate of a whistleblower & transparency bill (SB53) share all private texts/emails about the bill (some involving former OAI employees) as the bill was debated
Quoting @jasonkwon
There’s quite a lot more to the story than this.
As everyone knows, we are actively defending against Elon in a lawsuit where he is trying to damage OpenAI for his own financial benefit.
Encode, the organization for which @_NathanCalvin serves as the General Counsel, was one of the first third parties - whose funding has not been fully disclosed - that quickly filed in support of Musk. For a safety policy organization to side with Elon (?), that raises legitimate questions about what is going on. We wanted to know, and still are curious to know, whether Encode is working in collaboration with third parties who have a commercial competitive interest adverse to OpenAI.
The stated narrative makes this sound like something it wasn’t.
1/ Subpoenas are to be expected, and it would be surprising if Encode did not get counsel on this from their lawyers. When a third party inserts themselves into active litigation, they are subject to standard legal processes. We issued a subpoena to ensure transparency around their involvement and funding. This is a routine step in litigation, not a separate legal action against Nathan or Encode.
2/ Subpoenas are part of how both sides seek information and gather facts for transparency; they don’t assign fault or carry penalties. Our goal was to understand the full context of why Encode chose to join Elon’s legal challenge.
3/ We’ve also been asking for some time who is funding their efforts connected to both this lawsuit and SB53, since they’ve publicly linked themselves to those initiatives. If they don’t have relevant information, they can simply respond that way.
4/ This is not about opposition to regulation or SB53. We did not oppose SB53; we provided comments for harmonization with other standards. We were also one of the first to sign the EU AIA COP, and still one of a few labs who test with the CAISI and UK AISI. We’ve also been clear with our own staff that they are free to express their takes on regulation, even if they disagree with the company, like during the 1047 debate (see thread below).
5/ We checked with our outside law firm about the deputy visit. The law firm used their standard vendor for service, and it’s quite common for deputies to also work as part-time process servers. We’ve been informed that they called Calvin ahead of time to arrange a time for him to accept service, so it should not have been a surprise.
6/ Our counsel interacted with Nathan’s counsel and by all accounts the exchanges were civil and professional on both sides. Nathan’s counsel denied they had materials in some cases and refused to respond in other cases. Discovery is now closed, and that’s that.
For transparency, below is the excerpt from the subpoena that lists all of the requests for production. People can judge for themselves what this was really focused on. Most of our questions still haven’t been answered.
────────
[2/3] See more context in Nathan's thread here - if OpenAI really have nothing to hide they'll explain why they did this too, not just sidestep the main allegation
Quoting @_NathanCalvin
OpenAI went beyond just subpoenaing Encode about Elon. OpenAI could (and did!) send a subpoena to Encode’s corporate address asking about our funders or communications with Elon (which don’t exist).
If OpenAI had stopped there, maybe you could argue it was in good faith. 5/15
────────
[3/3] Worse, it's a whistleblower and transparency bill! I'm sure there's a lot of people who spoke to Encode, likely including both current and former OpenAI employees, who were critical of OpenAI and would prefer to not have their privacy violated by sharing texts with OpenAI

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5)
summary:
This was a great paper to help with - I really did not expect it to be this easy to interpret what a model was narrowly finetuned on, nor for it to be so easy to automate!
IMO anyone using narrowly finetuned model organisms should mix in neutral data to reduce this effect
Quoting @jkminder
New paper: Finetuning on narrow domains leaves traces behind. By looking at the difference in activations before and after finetuning, we can interpret what it was finetuned for. And so can our interpretability agent! 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G3ticyqWkAAWkw9.png

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5)
summary:
It's lovely to see an old school, deep dive mech interp analysis on a real model! (Claude 3.5 Haiku). This is both much more convoluted and more comprehensible than I expected! And so pretty
This seems the most complex behaviour yet understood at real depth, nice work!
Quoting @wesg52
New paper! We reverse engineered the mechanisms underlying Claude Haiku’s ability to perform a simple “perceptual” task. We discover beautiful feature families and manifolds, clean geometric transformations, and distributed attention algorithms!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G3zKeazbAAAHn4O.jpg

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5)
summary:
Great work! It's really nice to see serious attempts to determine what it means for a language model to believe something or not. I think current LLMs are approaching being coherent enough for "believe" to be a reasonable word, but there's a lot of room for conceptual clarity here
Quoting @stewpervised
Techniques like synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF) have been proposed to modify AI beliefs. But do AIs really believe the implanted facts?
In a new paper, we study this empirically. We find:
1. SDF sometimes (not always) implants genuine beliefs
2. But other techniques do not
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G34bchtawAAhz1j.jpg

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] I'm very excited about this paper. A problem with evaluating LLMs for safety is if they notice they're in a test they act well - this already happens!
We made and release a realistic model that acts differently when tested, and subtracting the "I'm in a test" vector fixes this!
Quoting @Tim_Hua_
Problem: AIs can detect when they are being tested and fake good behavior.
Can we suppress the “I’m being tested” concept & make them act normally?
Yes! In a new paper, we show that subtracting this concept vector can elicit real-world behavior even when normal prompting fails.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G4hJyJBa8AAGUUw.jpg
────────
[2/2] The core issue with studying eval awareness is that we lack a ground truth. Only the latest frontier models show significant eval awareness, and nothing open source. By designing a realistic model organism we can study this issue now!

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] The GDM mechanistic interpretability team has pivoted to a new approach: pragmatic interpretability
Our post details how we now do research, why now is the time to pivot, why we expect this way to have more impact and why we think other interp researchers should follow suit
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fnxf2agAA4isM.jpg
────────
[2/8] Core principles:
Doing good research is hard, it's easy to be misled
Doing *impactful* research is harder - we care about AGI but it doesn't exist yet!
Solution: measure progress with empirical proxy tasks that track progress towards a North Star
Post:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fnyata8AAoees.jpg
────────
[3/8] Does this mean giving up on curiosity? No! Curiosity is a powerful driver of research progress. But exciting ≠ true, let alone important. It needs grounding:
- Start in an important setting
- Time-box exploration (eg 2 wks)
- Fail fast - eventually find a proxy task, or move on
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7FnzX9bQAAFNWV.jpg
────────
[4/8] Why pivot?
- Models are better, we can study safety problems directly
- Ambitious reverse-engineering work gave underwhelming results
- Most techniques struggle on frontier behaviours
- We see neglected paths to impact via pragmatism
The best interp work is already pragmatic:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fn0PeacAAODsZ.jpg
────────
[5/8] We advocate method minimalism: start solving your proxy task with the simplest methods (e.g. prompting, steering, probing, reading chain-of-thought). Black box interp has had a great year!
Introduce complexity or design new methods only if baselines fail
Just do what works!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fn1HVagAEMLBr.jpg
────────
[6/8] How do we choose projects?
Our top priority is ensuring that AGI goes well, and we start there. But that includes a lot!
We filter according to the comparative advantages of mech interp researchers, which are far broader than "classic" mech interp
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fn2AKaMAE1z9j.jpg
────────
[7/8] Is this really mech interp?
No, probably not. But that's the wrong question. We're asking: how can mech interp *researchers* have the most impact?
Our priority is to help AGI go well. Semantics are irrelevant. Just do what works.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fn24za4AARnJs.jpg
────────
[8/8] What does having an impact here actually look like? For that, see our companion piece, with our takes on promising research directions and theories of change, as well as robustly useful settings that look good from many perspectives.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fn3xdaIAEcKeV.jpg

summary:
[1/3] A key frontier in interp is basic science of CoT. Sampling is random and non differentiable breaking normal interp. But there's a ton of low hanging fruit!
Simple resampling suggests blackmail isn't driven by self preservation, can interpret unfaithful CoT and beats manual edits
Quoting @uzaymacar
New paper: You can’t interpret LLM reasoning from one chain-of-thought. You must study a distribution of possible trajectories!
Repeated sampling reveals: self-preservation doesn’t drive LLM blackmail, unfaithful reasoning reflects a biased path, & resampling steers behavior. 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1995890689947959298/img/ycDP2zV2GeO_BrGd.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/1995890689947959298/vid/avc1/576x270/NhJIAGTJZW3cTVpl.mp4?tag=16

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Pragmatic interp is a research philosophy, not an agenda. It's about how to avoid common mistakes and produce true and impactful insights. You can apply it to whatever problems you want.
Also, the posts are not just on post training problems! There's lots of other examples
Quoting @aryaman2020
the major flaw of “pragmatic interpretability” imo: the problems that this approach wants to work on are the same problems posttraining researchers work on, except posttraining researchers don’t have to restrict themselves to specific research methodologies (e.g. interp)
────────
[2/2] Problems I'm excited about that I do not think standard post training researchers work on:
- Why did the model take this action? (Eg trying to escape the data center, or blackmailing)
- Efficient inference time monitors
- Extracting secret knowledge
- Which sentence in the CoT drove its actions
- Was my eval invalidated because the model knew it was being tested?
- How can I suppress eval awareness at inference time?
- How can we "read the CoT" of a latent reasoning model?
- Diagnosing what was learned during finetuning to inform better development of methods
- Understanding how to filter pretraining data to prevent pathologies like emergent misalignment
- Eliciting weird or sketchy model behaviours
- Generating adversarial examples better and more realistically
- Debugging causes of weird model failures

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] Interpretability agents are a big deal for researchers. But they're a pain - research is so custom!
Seer has many quality of life improvements to make research with agents easy. It's hackable & extensible, to enable as much research as possible, incl weird cursed techniques!
Quoting @AJakkli
Seer is a small repo for interp researchers working on/with agents. Makes it easier to set up environments, equip agents with your techniques, and build on papers. Fixes a lot of the annoying stuff from using Claude Code out of the box.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G8iaHNDWcAATIeq.png
────────
[2/4] It's hackable enough to work for a wide range of work:
- Replicate @Jack_W_Lindsey's model introspection work
- Build a black box auditing agent like Petri
- Give Petri steering
- Elicit secret knowledge from @bartoszcyw's models
- Do black box model diffing with SAEs
- And more!
────────
[3/4] Why am I excited about interp agents?
1. Interp needs to be scalable to matter on frontier LLMs
2. Even now, interp agents can teach us a lot - they're useful!
3. They're also an objective way to evaluate interpretability techniques - do agents with your technique do better?
────────
[4/4] Check out seer here:

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] I'm excited to release Gemma Scope 2: a comprehensive set of interpretability tools on Gemma 3. SAEs & transcoders on every layer of every model!
Gemma 3 27B shows lots of rich safety-relevant behaviour I want to enable deep dives into what's really going on
Check out our demo!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G8zrNxZaMAAJseg.jpg
Quoting @calsmcdougall
Google DeepMind is releasing Gemma Scope 2: SAEs and transcoders on every layer of every Gemma 3 model, 270M-27B, base & chat.
We hope this enables deep dives into complex model behavior, for more ambitious open source safety & interpretability work!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G8zb2CVW8AA1t_s.jpg
────────
[2/7] Demo:
I see two main ways of using Gemma Scope 2 to study model behaviour:
- Augment an existing investigation by seeing the concepts the model is using and how important they are
- Do a deep dive into mechanisms to try to understand underlying circuits
────────
[3/7] To see the concepts, you can just use a single residual stream SAE on a middle layer - try it on Neuronpedia!
But key concepts can only appear in different parts of the model! So we include an experimental weakly causal cross-coder on 4 spaced out layers, to study all at once
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G8zrPd8agAIifyP.jpg
────────
[4/7] For deep dives, we include transcoders on every layer to let you form attribution graphs. Neuronpedia support, incl for generating your own coming soon.
I'm excited to see what we can learn from such deep dives that can't be learned via simpler methods
────────
[5/7] A common question is, what does this have to do with pragmatic interpretability? Aren't SAEs dead?
While I think SAEs have been overhyped, the optimal amount of hype is far from zero! SAEs & transcoders are great exploratory tools to understand a model's concepts and circuits
Quoting @NeelNanda5
The GDM mechanistic interpretability team has pivoted to a new approach: pragmatic interpretability
Our post details how we now do research, why now is the time to pivot, why we expect this way to have more impact and why we think other interp researchers should follow suit
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Fnxf2agAA4isM.jpg
────────
[6/7] Notably, SAEs and co have major up front costs but are cheap to use. For any given project in isolation they're often not worth making, but I'm excited to help make it so that the community can ignore those and just use this useful tool
────────
[7/7] Check out Neuronpedia's great demo here, including a nice GUI for using Gemma Scope 2 yourself, and links to learn more:
And congratulations to @calsmcdougall for making this project happen nearly solo!

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] Helping with this project was a fascinating view into what it takes to get safety work used in the real world. Even a simple technique like probes had tons of room for improvement and required lots of hard work from Arthur and many across Google. It really keeps research grounded
Quoting @ArthurConmy
Our new @GoogleDeepMind paper studies novel activation probe architectures for classifying real-world misuse risks.
Our research has informed live deployments of probes in Gemini. 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_CgVKLWMAc1sTl.jpg
────────
[2/5] The bulk of my team's research is not production facing right now, but safety research only matters if it's eventually used! So this was a very educational experience on that front.
I discussed some of my lessons on the 80000 Hours podcast:
────────
[3/5] - Simplicity: Actually using anything novel in a prod setting is extremely hard and complex. Any additional bit of complexity is costly
- Reality is messy: To do things in the real world, a bunch of key considerations arise "do my probes generalise to long-context or multi-turn"
────────
[4/5] - Side effects: Your techniques need to work *and* not degrade other things. Your cyber-crime classifier can't fire on 10% of user traffic!
- Efficiency: It's incredibly useful to have cheaper techniques - if your technique is being used on every Gemini call, it really adds up
────────
[5/5] None of these are particularly surprising, in hindsight, but many researchers neglect them!
Check out the paper here - we tried to make it a useful guide re how to actually use probes in the real world:

I had a lot of fun working on this paper - we found an elegant story for why subliminal learning happens!
A key intuition in interpretability is that basically every interesting phenomena in LLMs boils down to adding a steering vector. Subliminal learning is no exception!
Quoting @camila_blank
Subliminal learning is when LLMs transmit traits (e.g. loving cats) through seemingly meaningless data. What’s going on?
We find a simple explanation: it's just steering vector distillation.
We explain which traits transfer and why subliminal learning fails across models.

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5)
summary:
This was a fascinating project - turns out that LLMs inherit a lot of traits from LLMs they're distilled from, including in subtle ways without clear semantic meaning. This has pretty interesting implications - safety problems in a model initialized with distillation may not be caused by the current post-training environments at all, but instead be a lingering issue caused by mistakes in previous post-training set ups, getting inherited through the generations despite ostensibly being fixed.
Quoting @JoshAEngels
Gemini has some weird traits: it gets confused about dates, blackmails in synthetic scenarios, and seems sad when it is gaslit.
In new work, we discover that these are “hereditary traits” that can be passed down through distillation. They are surprisingly hard to filter out!
🧵

title: Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5)
summary:
Very interesting commentary contrasting our work trying to explain subliminal learning with prior work, check it out:
Quoting @nhaghtal
1/ I enjoyed reading “Subliminal Learning Is Steering Vector Distillation”. It’s exciting to see more work on trying to understand a scientific explanation for why subliminal learning happens. Thank you also for citing our work “Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity” (arXiv:2602.04863, ICML 2026). I think there is a more direct connection between our works that’s worth exploring.
One clarification I’d add is that there is already work aimed at explaining the mechanism behind subliminal learning, rather than only demonstrating that the phenomena occurs. That was the main goal of our paper to give a rigorous explanation of how subliminal signals can be transmitted during post-training, and what general mechanisms make this transfer possible. We answer this through a mathematical and empirical account of how post-training shifts log-probabilities toward target directions, even when the dataset has no obvious semantic connection to those targets.
